delinquency.conventional_30plus_share.unit: fraction of conventional one-to-four-unit loans one payment or more past due and not in foreclosure, seasonally adjusted, quarter end
delinquency.conventional_30plus_share.terms: MBA press release, read as MBA's own NewsLink reprint. The National Delinquency Survey itself (its data tables and report) is licensed by MBA and was not used; figures are quoted with attribution to MBA's National Delinquency Survey.
delinquency.conventional_30plus_share.note: MBA National Delinquency Survey, second quarter of 2026 (press release of 13 August 2026): conventional 2.72%, down 3 bp on the quarter and up 12 bp on the year. The press release itself is at mba.org/news-and-research/newsroom/news/2026/08/13/mortgage-delinquencies-decrease-slightly-in-the-second-quarter-of-2026, which answers automated fetches with 403; this is MBA's own reprint of it. A credit-bureau measure reads lower: FHFA's NMDB has 2026Q2 Enterprise loans at 0.7% 30-89 days and 0.3% 90 days or more past due.

delinquency.all_loans_30plus_share_sa.unit: fraction of all one-to-four-unit loans; total, buckets and types seasonally adjusted, serious delinquency not, foreclosure as MBA reports it
delinquency.all_loans_30plus_share_sa.terms: MBA press release, read as MBA's own NewsLink reprint. The National Delinquency Survey itself (its data tables and report) is licensed by MBA and was not used; figures are quoted with attribution to MBA's National Delinquency Survey.
delinquency.all_loans_30plus_share_sa.note: MBA National Delinquency Survey, second quarter of 2026: 4.37% of loans one payment or more past due, seasonally adjusted (30 days 2.21%, 60 days 0.73%, 90 days or more 1.43%), down 7 bp on the quarter and up 44 bp on the year; 0.67% in foreclosure; foreclosure started on 0.2% in the quarter; 90 days or more or in foreclosure 2.06%, not seasonally adjusted. The buckets sum to the total. A seasonally adjusted stock is a level to compare a sample against, not a monthly rate.

delinquency.roll_current_to_30.unit: fraction of mortgage accounts current at one quarter end that are 30-60 days late (or 90 days or more late) at the next
delinquency.roll_current_to_30.terms: New York Fed Terms of Use (newyorkfed.org/privacy/termsofuse): reuse permitted with the attribution "New York Fed Consumer Credit Panel / Equifax"; modifications must be labeled and not attributed to the New York Fed. The fractions here are the published percents divided by 100 and rounded.
delinquency.roll_current_to_30.note: New York Fed Household Debt and Credit Report, 2026Q2, "Quarterly Transition Rates for Current Mortgage Accounts" (report page 15). A credit-report measure over a 0.1% sample of people with a credit report; mortgage accounts include closed-end home equity installment loans. No public source gives a monthly roll from current to 30 days. A loan that goes 30 days late and cures inside the quarter is not counted here, so the monthly hazard is more than a third of the quarterly figure. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac loan-level performance data would measure the monthly roll; their terms need counsel first and they were not used.

delinquency.cure_from_30.unit: fraction of mortgage accounts 30-60 days late at one quarter end that are current (or 90 days or more late) at the next
delinquency.cure_from_30.terms: New York Fed Terms of Use (newyorkfed.org/privacy/termsofuse): reuse permitted with the attribution "New York Fed Consumer Credit Panel / Equifax"; modifications must be labeled and not attributed to the New York Fed. The fractions here are the published percents divided by 100 and rounded.
delinquency.cure_from_30.note: New York Fed Household Debt and Credit Report, 2026Q2, "Quarterly Transition Rates for 30-60 Day Late Mortgage Accounts" (report page 16). The remainder (about 42% in 2026Q2) is still 30-60 days late a quarter later, or left the panel. Same measure and caveats as delinquency.roll_current_to_30; no public monthly cure rate was found.

delinquency.roll_30_to_60.unit: fraction of loans 30 days delinquent at one month end that are 60 days delinquent at the next
delinquency.roll_30_to_60.note: No public source publishes a monthly 30-to-60 roll: ICE's monthly First Look press release gives delinquency counts and cures but no roll rates (the July 2026 release, ir.theice.com, 25 August 2026), and Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac loan-level performance data, which would measure it, need counsel first. The value is MBA's second-quarter 2026 60-day bucket over its 30-day bucket (0.73% / 2.21% = 0.33; delinquency.all_loans_30plus_share_sa), which equals the monthly roll only if both stocks are steady. Cross-check: the New York Fed has 15.4% of 30-60 day accounts at 90 days or more one quarter later (delinquency.cure_from_30).

payment.day_of_month.unit: fraction of installments, on loans current at the due date, by the day of the due month the payment arrives
payment.day_of_month.note: No public source gives when in the month mortgage payments arrive; servicers hold it, and the loan-level performance data Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac publish (whose terms need counsel first) report a monthly status, not an arrival day. Assumed: due on the 1st with a 15-day grace period, so a payment received by the 16th is on time and a late charge falls from the 17th; the bulk paid on or just after the due day by autopay and bill pay, a tail through the grace period, and a small share not paid in the month. The bins sum to one; payment.late_within_grace_share, payment.late_after_grace_share and payment.missed_month_share are sums of them.

payment.late_within_grace_share.unit: fraction of installments, on loans current at the due date, received after the due day and within the grace period
payment.late_within_grace_share.note: The sum of payment.day_of_month's bins from day 2 to day 16. Not public, for the reason given there.

payment.late_after_grace_share.unit: fraction of installments, on loans current at the due date, not received by the end of the grace period (each one a late charge)
payment.late_after_grace_share.note: The sum of payment.day_of_month's bins from day 17 on, the month missed included. No public source gives a late-charge rate; the CFPB's supervisory findings on late fees (docs/synthetic-data-defects.md, D-03) are about fees charged in error, not how often one is owed.

payment.partial_share.unit: fraction of receipts: short of the installment due (held in suspense), and returned after posting (an ACH debit or check reversed)
payment.partial_share.note: No public source gives either rate for mortgage payments. Both are kept low on the assumption that most installments arrive by scheduled bank debit or bill pay. Returned payments sit under this key because the key list has no other place for them.

payment.curtailment_share.unit: fraction of installments carrying extra principal
payment.curtailment_share.note: No public aggregate counts curtailments. Loan-level performance data from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac could measure them; their terms need counsel first and they were not used. Assumed: a small share of borrowers add principal most months and a few send an occasional lump sum.

payment.missed_month_share.unit: fraction of loan-months, on loans current at the due date, in which no installment arrives by month end
payment.missed_month_share.note: payment.day_of_month's not_in_month bin. Bounded by two public figures. The New York Fed has 0.84% of current accounts 30-60 days late a quarter later (delinquency.roll_current_to_30); every one of them missed a month in that quarter, and loans that missed and cured inside it are not counted, so a third of it, 0.28% a month, is a floor. MBA's 2.21% 30-day stock (delinquency.all_loans_30plus_share_sa), which also holds loans that stay one payment behind, is a ceiling. To be tested against both through the delinquency-stock and quarterly-transitions acceptance tests.

contacts.per_loan_year.unit: call center inquiries per loan per year
contacts.per_loan_year.terms: CFPB publication, a work of the U.S. Government (17 U.S.C. 105).
contacts.per_loan_year.note: CFPB, Mortgage Servicing COVID-19 Pandemic Response Metrics (May 2022), sixteen servicers, May through December 2021: about 21 million loans (section 2.1) and 3.32 to 3.64 million inquiries a month, nearly 28 million in all (section 2.2). Derived: 28 million / 21 million loans over eight months is 2.0 a loan-year; 3.32 and 3.64 million a month are 1.9 and 2.08. Limits: servicers counted inquiries differently (some counted calls ended in the IVR), the period is the end of pandemic forbearance, and the report gives no split by delinquency status.

contacts.handle_time_minutes.terms: CFPB publication, a work of the U.S. Government (17 U.S.C. 105).
contacts.handle_time_minutes.note: Same report, section 2.2: reported average handle time ranged from 4.3 to 19.8 minutes across servicers and call centers by month; no pooled average is given. Average speed to answer was 2.95 minutes counting time in the IVR and 1.46 minutes not counting it. The report explains part of the spread by servicers reporting call centers with different functions separately.

contacts.inbound_reason_mix.unit: fraction of servicing complaints by reason
contacts.inbound_reason_mix.terms: CFPB Consumer Complaint Database, public data under CC0 (the API's own metadata). The CFPB says it is not a statistical sample of consumers' experiences.
contacts.inbound_reason_mix.note: Mortgage complaints received in 2025, by issue and sub-issue, origination issues (applying for a mortgage, closing) left out; every credit-reporting issue is one reason. 20,049 complaints. A skewed proxy for why borrowers call: a complaint is a call that went wrong, so disputes (escrow, loss mitigation, foreclosure) are likely over-represented and routine calls (a payment amount, a statement, a payoff figure) under-represented. Shares are rounded to four places; the largest absorbs the rounding.

escrow.share_of_loans.unit: fraction of mortgaged owner-occupied units whose payment includes real estate taxes
escrow.share_of_loans.note: The ACS asks it (whether the regular mortgage payment includes real estate taxes, and insurance), but no ACS summary table publishes the answer; it is in the PUMS microdata only. Reading it needs the 2024 1-year PUMS housing file (csv_hus.zip, 251.5 MB, www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/data/pums/2024/1-Year/) or the Census API, which on 2026-10-23 refused requests without a key. Neither was done here. The value is an assumption until the PUMS share is computed.

escrow.tax_annual_median.unit: dollars a year, median real estate taxes paid, owner-occupied units
escrow.tax_annual_median.terms: U.S. Census Bureau data product, a work of the U.S. Government (17 U.S.C. 105). Cite as U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 1-Year Estimates, with the table number.
escrow.tax_annual_median.note: ACS 2024 1-year, table B25103 (Mortgage Status by Median Real Estate Taxes Paid), United States: $3,580 for units with a mortgage. The 2025 1-year tables were not in the Census Bureau's summary-file directory on 2026-10-23. A median across the country; the spread by state is wide, and the generator should draw around it rather than assign it.

escrow.insurance_annual_median.unit: dollars a year, median homeowners insurance cost, owner-occupied units with a mortgage
escrow.insurance_annual_median.terms: U.S. Census Bureau data product, a work of the U.S. Government (17 U.S.C. 105). Cite as U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 1-Year Estimates, with the table number.
escrow.insurance_annual_median.note: ACS 2024 1-year, table B25141 (Homeowners Insurance Costs by Mortgage Status, Yearly), United States, units with a mortgage. The table gives a distribution, not a median: the median here ($1,450) is interpolated linearly inside the bin that holds the middle unit. The distribution's shares are the table's counts over its with-mortgage total; the lowest bin is under $100 and the highest $4,000 or more.

escrow.tax_growth_yoy.unit: fraction a year, change in the median real estate taxes paid by units with a mortgage
escrow.tax_growth_yoy.terms: U.S. Census Bureau data product, a work of the U.S. Government (17 U.S.C. 105). Cite as U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 1-Year Estimates, with the table number.
escrow.tax_growth_yoy.note: Derived by comparing table B25103's US median for units with a mortgage across ACS 1-year releases 2021 to 2024 (the same file name for each year under www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/<year>/table-based-SF/data/1YRData/). Nominal dollars. A change in the median across different households each year, not the change in one property's bill.

escrow.insurance_growth_yoy.unit: fraction a year, change in the interpolated median homeowners insurance cost of units with a mortgage
escrow.insurance_growth_yoy.terms: U.S. Census Bureau data product, a work of the U.S. Government (17 U.S.C. 105). Cite as U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 1-Year Estimates, with the table number.
escrow.insurance_growth_yoy.note: Derived from table B25141's 2023 and 2024 1-year releases, each median interpolated as in escrow.insurance_annual_median. The table starts in 2023, so this is one year's change. Nominal dollars, different households each year.

arm.share_of_outstanding.unit: fraction of active closed-end first-lien mortgages that are adjustable-rate
arm.share_of_outstanding.terms: FHFA NMDB Aggregate Statistics, published as public data under CC0 1.0 (data.gov catalog entry). Cite as FHFA, National Mortgage Database Aggregate Statistics.
arm.share_of_outstanding.note: FHFA NMDB Outstanding Residential Mortgage Statistics, national, 2026Q2: ARMs originated within four years plus those originated earlier. "loans" is weighted by count (VALUE1), "upb" by unpaid balance (VALUE2). Other conventional (portfolio and jumbo) loans carry most of them.

mi.share_of_loans.unit: fractions: of loans (government), of unpaid balance (private MI), of 2025 Enterprise originations (CLTV over 80)
mi.share_of_loans.terms: U.S. Mortgage Insurers' annual report as summarized by MBA NewsLink (August 2025), quoted with attribution; FHFA NMDB under CC0 for the denominators.
mi.share_of_loans.note: No public source counts the loans carrying private mortgage insurance. U.S. Mortgage Insurers put outstanding mortgages with active private MI at nearly $1.6 trillion at the end of 2024, more than $1.4 trillion of it GSE-backed. Over FHFA NMDB's 2024Q4 unpaid balances (Enterprise $6,558.5 billion, other conventional $3,084.7 billion) that is the share of conventional balance shown, by dollars and not by loans. Government loans (insured, guaranteed or made directly by a federal agency; 23.6% of loans in NMDB 2026Q2) carry no private MI. Of 2025 Enterprise originations, the share with combined LTV over 80 (NMDB new-mortgage statistics) is an upper bound on the share that needed MI at origination.

book.note_rate_distribution.unit: fraction of active closed-end first-lien mortgages by contract interest rate (bucket bounds in percent)
book.note_rate_distribution.terms: FHFA NMDB Aggregate Statistics, published as public data under CC0 1.0 (data.gov catalog entry). Cite as FHFA, National Mortgage Database Aggregate Statistics.
book.note_rate_distribution.note: FHFA NMDB Outstanding Residential Mortgage Statistics, national, 2026Q2, all mortgages: the contract rate at origination of every active loan (an ARM's rate at origination, not today's). Buckets are under 3%, 3.00-3.99, 4.00-4.99, 5.00-5.99, 6% and over. The published shares are rounded to 0.1 point and may sum to 0.999 or 1.001.

book.ltv_distribution.unit: fraction of loans by loan-to-value (bucket bounds in percent)
book.ltv_distribution.terms: FHFA NMDB Aggregate Statistics, published as public data under CC0 1.0 (data.gov catalog entry). Cite as FHFA, National Mortgage Database Aggregate Statistics.
book.ltv_distribution.note: FHFA NMDB, national. Mark-to-market: active loans in 2026Q2, current balance over the origination value moved by FHFA's house price index (Outstanding Residential Mortgage Statistics). At origination: 2025 Enterprise acquisitions by combined LTV (New Residential Mortgage Statistics, nmdb-new-mortgage-statistics-national-census-areas-annual.zip). Published shares are rounded to 0.1 point.

book.loan_age_distribution.unit: fraction of active closed-end first-lien mortgages by years since origination
book.loan_age_distribution.terms: FHFA NMDB Aggregate Statistics, published as public data under CC0 1.0 (data.gov catalog entry). Cite as FHFA, National Mortgage Database Aggregate Statistics.
book.loan_age_distribution.note: FHFA NMDB Outstanding Residential Mortgage Statistics, national, 2026Q2: up to 4 years, 4.01-7, 7.01-10, over 10. The 2020-2021 refinance wave sits in the 4-7 year bucket in 2026.

refi.pmms_30y_series.unit: percent, the survey's weekly average 30-year fixed rate (week as M/D/YYYY, the Thursday it was published)
refi.pmms_30y_series.terms: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey: "Information from this document may be used with proper attribution"; "Alteration of this document or its content is strictly prohibited" (freddiemac.com/pmms; terms at freddiemac.com/terms). Attribute as Freddie Mac, Primary Mortgage Market Survey. Rows are copied as published, dates in the file's own form.
refi.pmms_30y_series.note: Weekly 30-year fixed rate from the first week of 2016 to the newest week on the fetch date. The points column (pmms30p) is left out; the rates are the file's own. A replay that shifts, rescales or splices this series to make synthetic rate paths is a use of altered content, and whether that is permitted is a question for counsel before any generator does it; using it as published, with attribution, is what the terms allow.

disaster.declarations_by_month.unit: count per calendar month of declaration date: distinct declarations by type, and designated areas under major disasters with Individual Assistance or Individuals and Households declared
disaster.declarations_by_month.terms: OpenFEMA terms: "This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA. The Federal Government or FEMA cannot vouch for the data or analyses derived from these data after the data have been retrieved from the Agency's website(s)." Cite the endpoint and version (DisasterDeclarationsSummaries v2) and the access date.
disaster.declarations_by_month.note: Counted from all 25,236 designated-area rows declared since 1 January 2016, through the last complete month. A disaster declared for several states counts once per state, because each state's declaration has its own number. The spike in March and April 2020 (108 emergencies, then 33 and 33 major disasters) is the COVID-19 declarations.

transfer.annual_rate.unit: fraction of loans whose servicing moves to another servicer in a year
transfer.annual_rate.note: No public source gives an annual servicing-transfer rate. Loan-level performance data from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac could measure it; their terms need counsel first and they were not used. The one public figure found is a lifetime floor: the CFPB's Data Point: Servicer Size in the Mortgage Market (2019, Appendix D) identifies 16% of NMDB loans as transferred at some point, and says the method may not pick up every transfer (https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_2019-servicer-size-mortgage-market_report.pdf). Spread over an average loan life of several years that is a few percent a year.

D-03.per: loan whose note caps the late fee below the state maximum

D-18.field: mortgage-insurance termination dates or original value

D-42.per: yes-or-no cell in a transfer package

defects.field_error_rates.unit: fraction of the stated unit carrying the planted defect
defects.field_error_rates.note: No public source gives how often each field is wrong (docs/synthetic-data-defects.md, Gaps and caveats); the only measured rates are aggregates (72% and 90% of loans needing correction in Ocwen's own reviews, an allegation; 0.0%, 3.3% and 11.4% financial-injury error rates in the Independent Foreclosure Review). These are the ten that page ranks first (eleven IDs; its ninth holds two) and its three runners-up. Each rate is per eligible unit and low enough that a defective loan stays the exception; D-43 is per package because one such cell aborts the whole batch. They stay a design choice until a subservicer's sample is in hand.
